column3: Joins following revelation, exclusive deity, and turning from association; directly frames the verse's source and warning.
Closest parallel: assigning another deity beside God culminates in being cast into severe punishment.
Broadens revelation as directed communication, but adds no direct association or final-punishment element.
Immediate preceding parallel supplies the same prohibition and a matching blame-and-abandonment consequence.
Supplies the resistant response to making the many deities one, clarifying the contested exclusivity.
Confirms revelation's character, but its terse formulation adds little beyond earlier revelation links.
Pairs recitation of revealed scripture with God's unmatched words; supports source-authority rather than the warning's outcome.
Its flight toward God forms a positive counterpart to refusing another deity.
A rebuke of corrupt judgment supports wisdom's corrective dimension, without the verse's central vocabulary.
Near-verbatim prohibition of another deity, now as a public warning; reinforces the closing command.
Contrasts the messenger's lack of blame with the blame assigned in 17:39, but is otherwise indirect.
Adds the linked pattern of expulsion, blame, and Hell behind the final consequence.
Restates the prohibition and adds God's sole judgment and return, extending its accountability frame.

Associates wisdom with abundant good and receptive understanding, but remains general.

Records attachment to multiple deities as resistance, a secondary counterpart to exclusive devotion.

Receiving words and repentance form a remote counterpart to revealed correction.
Mutual blame is a limited lexical and ethical echo.
The verse's will statement and rejected reading do not materially illuminate 17:39.

A general punishment statement adds only background for the warning.
Rejects fabricated partners, but the wisdom epithet adds little beyond stronger direct parallels.
Opposition to God and messenger ending in Hell supports the consequence motif, though without association.
A demand for a treasure has no meaningful relation to the focus verse.
The path of Hell offers generic consequence support only.
The command to cast in the Moses narrative is not interpretively connected.
Hell for rejecting signs and mocking messengers extends the accountability setting of revealed wisdom.

The plea against rancor is an ethical restraint but does not clarify 17:39.

Command not to obey opponents supports restraint, but not the verse's specific revelation-association nexus.
Captives, recompense, and forgiveness do not add a usable connection.
The trial of Solomon has only a shared casting verb.
Proportionate spending parallels the surrounding wisdom instructions, but remains indirect.

A proposed barrier against corrupters concerns restraint only at a distant practical level.

Solomon's rejection of a gift does not illuminate the focus verse.
Tranquility and divine wisdom give only an abstract corrective-wisdom resonance.
Preferring others over self shows the ethical self-restraint that the surrounding wisdom injunctions cultivate.
Refusal to alter revelation grounds its authority and obedience, a secondary support for 17:39's source claim.
The self-reproaching soul echoes blame but does not determine its meaning here.
Divine might and wisdom are general attributes; the link is already better established elsewhere.
Near-parallel prohibition of another deity with punishment, reinforcing the warning's direct force.
Excuses being put forward has no substantive relation to the focus verse.
Protects revealed signs from diversion and repeats the anti-association stance.
Casting order in the Moses contest has no interpretive value here.

Bad judgment and evil deeds are an indirect contrast to divine wisdom.

Refusing worship leads to entering Hell humbled, supplying a close consequence counterpart.

Turning from the Book's judgment contrasts with the focus verse, but only generally.
Continuity of revelation across earlier recipients supports its stable divine source.
The magicians' response remains a separate narrative use of casting.

Joseph's family entering Egypt safely is unrelated.

Frames messengership through recitation, purification, and teaching the Book and wisdom.

States that the Book and wisdom were sent down and taught to the addressee.
Limits the messenger to what is revealed, supporting the authority of 17:39's disclosed wisdom.

Names association without divine authority among prohibited excesses.
Makes following the revelation the response to demands for other signs.
Shows how other authorities may be treated as lords beside God.

Connects revealed discourse with warning and divine accountability.
Presents the Quran as revelation that supplies otherwise unavailable knowledge.
Rejects association through inherited prophetic allegiance to God alone.

States that the Reminder was sent down so its content could be made clear.
Forbids taking two deities and grounds fear in God's singularity.
Treats revelation as divinely sequenced and contested, supporting its authority.

Locates judgment of inward states with the Lord, extending the sequence's accountability.
Adds the duty of giving due rights within the wisdom material summarized in 17:39.
Condemns waste as alignment with devils, clarifying the practical restraints in the sequence.
Adds a restrained and gracious response when provision cannot be given.
Places provision and constraint under the Lord's knowing, seeing determination.
Forbids killing children from fear of poverty and anchors provision in God.
Forbids approaching sexual indecency as a corrupt path.
Forbids unlawful killing and regulates redress, extending wisdom as moral limit.
Commands care for orphans, fulfillment of covenant, and accountable commitments.
Commands full measure and balance, a concrete instance of wise rectitude.
Forbids pursuing what one lacks knowledge of and makes faculties accountable.
Forbids arrogant conduct, completing the sequence of corrective restraints.
Labels those preceding practices as evil before the summary in 17:39.
Opposes pressure to divert the messenger from what was revealed.
Shows the revealed gift remains dependent on divine mercy and cannot be presumed secure.
Affirms God's sole judgment and denies any partner in it.
Joins revelation with the proclamation of one God and rejection of associating partners.
Commands exclusive worship by denying any peer to the Lord.
States God's singular deityhood and the consequent command of worship.
Makes the one-God worship command the common content of prior revelation.
Condenses the revelation to the declaration that the deity is one.
Contrasts God's reality and supremacy with what is invoked besides Him.
Denies God has a child or any deity alongside Him, with a causal argument against plurality.
Affirms God's transcendence and singular lordship after accountability is stated.
Denies God any partner in dominion and affirms comprehensive determination.
The messenger's complaint about abandoning the Quran sharpens the stakes of revealed guidance.
Commands striving by means of the Quran, extending revealed discourse into action.
Moves from the anti-association warning to warning one's nearest kin.
Provides the conduct toward those who disobey the warning.
Challenges the addition of any deity alongside God after His saving acts.

Uses the ordered earth to reject the claim of any deity alongside God.
Uses answered distress and succession on earth to reject the claim of any deity alongside God.
Uses guidance through darkness and winds to reject the claim of any deity alongside God.
Uses origination and return to reject the claim of any deity alongside God.
Affirms that He is God alone, with praise, judgment, and return belonging to Him.
Names association as a grave wrong within a wisdom teaching from Luqman.
Regulates conduct when parents press for association while preserving refusal of it.
Commands following what the Lord has revealed to the prophet.
Challenges alleged partners by denying their share in heaven and earth.
Denies any creator and provider other than God, supporting exclusive devotion.
Rejects taking other deities because their intercession cannot avert harm.
Records refusal of the declaration that there is no deity but God, clarifying the opposed stance.
Commands sincere worship of God on the basis of the revealed Book.
Defines religion as belonging sincerely to God and rejects intermediary devotion.
Restates the command to worship God with religion made sincere to Him.
Combines exclusive, sincere worship with the prophet's declaration of obedience.
Rejects being commanded to worship other than God despite revealed guidance.
Contrasts calling to God with being called to associate what has no knowledge or warrant.
Links revealed proclamation with the declaration that the deity is one.
Calls for inquiry whether any deities besides the Merciful were ever authorized for worship.
Characterizes invocation besides God as the furthest error.
States worship of God as the created purpose, supporting the positive pole of the warning.
Introduces the named alternative objects of devotion challenged in the following passage.
Continues the presentation of the alternative objects subjected to critique.
Exposes the unequal allocation projected onto God in the surrounding critique of false deities.
Rejects that projected allocation as unjust.
Denies the authority of named objects and contrasts them with guidance from the Lord.
Reserves places of worship for God and forbids calling anyone with Him.

Affirms the Lord of east and west, no deity but Him, and commands reliance on Him.
Declares God's absolute oneness, the core premise of the prohibition.
Affirms God's self-sufficiency, excluding dependency shared with a rival deity.
Denies progeny relations that could support a plural divine scheme.
